Acapulco (port locode MXACA) is a large port city and Mexico's fun capital and largest Pacific resort. As destination, it offers superb weather with an average 360 days of sunshine a year and amazing beaches. City's urban area is approx 85 km2 (33 mi2), and its population - around 700,000 (metro over 800,000).

In April 2026, Acapulco Cruise Port was leased by Global Ports Holding (GPH). The 24-year concession agreement marked GPH’s first Mexican port concession. The deal was signed with the ASIPONA Acapulco (National Port System Administration) and includes the operation and development of the cruise terminal (within a concession period) through phased investments by GPH (Turkey-based, family-run corporation, ranked the world's largest cruise port operator).

Located on a deepwater, semicircular bay, the city has the best harbour waterway on Mexico's Pacific coast. Acapulco runs along a narrow land strip between the bay and surrounding mountains. The most popular beaches and hotels are to the east and around the bay - Condesa, Icacos, Playas Hornos, Hornitos. A very popular cliff diving destination is Le Quebrada.

Acapulco harbor was discovered in 1531 by Hernan Cortes (1485-1547, Spanish conquistador/conqueror) and the settlement was established in 1550 as an important seaport for Spanish galleons (large wooden warships) sailing between Spain and the American territories. Sea traffic dwindled following Mexico gaining independence in 1821. Local tourism started to develop since 1927 when a paved road over mountains connected Pacific Mexico's first resort city. Today, tourism is the largest economic contributor, with most of it centred on Acapulco Bay. Over 70% of Acapulco's population is involved in commerce, and most of it relates to tourism and the cruise port. Manufacturing and mining employ nearly 1/5. Under 5% is agriculture.

Acapulco is one of Mexico's oldest coastal tourist destinations, booming during the 1950s as a vacation destination for US millionaires and Hollywood stars. In recent years, tourists face problems with corrupt police stealing money by extortion and threatening tourists with jail. Sadly, once a premium resort vacation destination, current-day Acapulco is largely associated with crime and corruption. The city is also plagued by violence from drug cartel wars. In 2015 were reported 903 murders - more than in any other Mexican city. The US State Department issued travel warnings for some Mexican areas, and Acapulco was also listed as risky.

In 2016, the cruise port handled a total of 18 ship calls. In 2017, the number grew to 32 (a 78% increase). The list of cruise companies with scheduled ships to Acapulco included Crystal, Hapag Lloyd, NCL, Oceania, RSSC-Regent, Saga UK, Silversea.

In 2017-2018, the cruise port had scheduled a total of 30 ship calls. For season 2017-2018, Holland America pulled from its Mexican Riviera cruise itineraries Port Acapulco due to concerns about violent crime in the region. The company (Carnival Corporation subsidiary) had scheduled 8 different itineraries to Pacific Mexico ports, but the popular resort destination Acapulco was scrapped and replaced with alternative Mexican ports. The changed Itineraries included 7 Panama Canal transits and 7 South American voyages.

During winter 2018-2019, the UK-based company CMV (Cruise and Maritime Voyages) homeported here the 1500-passenger liner Magellan. CMV's Acapulco roundtrip program included itineraries visiting the most popular Mexican Riviera ports Ixtapa-Zihuatanejo, Manzanillo, Puerto Vallarta, Cabo San Lucas (Baja California).

A USD 1 billion development plan (2017-2022) includes cruise port upgrades, major resorts renovations (Pierre Mundo Imperial, Princess Mundo Imperial), building new airport terminal, new hotels, shops, restaurants, amusement park, tennis stadium, medical center. The project includes:

  • Intense Emotion (space adventure attraction with suspension bridges, extreme rides, restaurant, world’s highest climbing wall / 40 m / 130 ft)
  • major hotel renovations (including Pierre Mundo Imperial, Princess Mundo Imperial)
  • new Princess Medical Center (sized 4,645 m2 / 50,000 ft2)
  • new tennis stadium, new eco-amusement park
  • In 2017 was inaugurated the XTASEA zip-line (world’s largest oversea zipline).
  • In 2018 was opened a new airport terminal.
  • City's infrastructure Improvements included several beautification projects.

In April 2017 was opened the USD 200 million macro-tunnel connecting Golden and Diamond districts. The 3,3 km long tunnel is Mexico's longest. The 3-line tunnel allows locals and tourists just 3 min commute travel (compared to the 1-hour drive via Avenida Escenica). The tunnel is monitored 24-hours via CCTVs, has modern fire protection system, temperature control (with 14 large fans), LED lighting, sound system (broadcasting important messages), emergency stations, 100% cell phone coverage, and can resist 8-Richter scale earthquake. Macro-tunnel passing costs around US$1.60 (residents) and US$3 (tourists).

During 2017's holiday season (Dec 20 - Jan 7) the city was visited by around 573,000 tourists, with average hotel occupancy over 81%. The port reported 3 cruise ship calls (Oceania Sirena, MS Europa, Norwegian Star) during the holidays and 40% increase in passenger shipping over 2016.

For season 2019, the cruise port had scheduled 30 ship calls (25 in 2018). Among the booked cruise companies were NCL-Norwegian, Oceania, RSSC-Regent, Ponant, Fred Olsen, Phoenix Reisen, CMV.

Acapulco cruise terminal

The Terminal Marítima Acapulco is a mid-tier cruise port primarily used as a call port  rather than a homeport. It has the ability to accommodate one to two large cruise ships (up to ~300 m) at dedicated alongside berths with adequate draft.

Terminal facilities are functional but relatively basic, providing essential passenger services such as restrooms, small retail outlets, and tour dispatch, without the scale or modern amenities of major cruise hubs. Its standout advantage is its central location in Acapulco, allowing cruise tourists to easily access the historic downtown, waterfront, and nearby attractions on foot, which significantly enhances its appeal despite infrastructure limitations.

The port operates as a multi-purpose facility shared with cargo traffic, which constrains scalability, but planned investments under a 24-year concession by GPH (2026-2050), including a new extended pier and upgraded terminal infrastructure.

In 2027 Q1 is planned the completion and inauguration of Acapulco's new cruise pier (length 350 m/1148 ft), allowing the berthing of larger cruise ships.

At a Glance

Independent sightseeing: Independent with some planning or transport. Acapulco is unusually convenient for a large resort city because cruise ships normally berth at the waterfront cruise terminal beside the historic center. Fuerte de San Diego, the malecón and Zócalo are all close enough for a short independent visit. La Quebrada and the traditional beaches are also nearby but are more practical by taxi.

For destinations farther around the bay or outside central Acapulco, an organized excursion or prearranged transport is preferable. Government travel advisories for Guerrero are restrictive because of security concerns, so passengers should check their own government's latest advice and follow guidance provided onboard.

Getting from the Cruise Port

Cruise ships normally dock directly at Acapulco Cruise Port, officially the Puerto Transatlántico Internacional Teniente José Azueta. Tendering is not the normal arrangement. The terminal is directly on the downtown waterfront, opposite the Fuerte de San Diego area and close to the old center.

The port is undergoing phased redevelopment under a new cruise-terminal operator, so the precise passenger exit and terminal facilities can change. Follow the route marked for your ship rather than relying solely on the mapped berth position.

  • Fuerte de San Diego: directly beside/opposite the cruise-terminal area and reachable in a few minutes on foot.
  • Zócalo and Acapulco Cathedral: roughly 0.7 km (0.4 mi) from the terminal, normally around 10 minutes on foot.
  • La Quebrada: roughly 2 km (1.2 mi) from the port. A taxi is preferable, particularly in the heat.
  • Caleta and Caletilla: approximately 3.5 km (2.2 mi) from the port; use a taxi rather than walking.
  • Capilla de la Paz: approximately 6 km (3.7 mi) away in the hills above the bay and requires road transport.

Taxis are the simplest option for attractions beyond downtown. Confirm the destination and fare before leaving. Acabús and local buses operate in the city, but for a short cruise call they are less convenient than walking or a taxi because routes, waiting times and traffic can reduce sightseeing time.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Fuerte de San Diego and Old Acapulco

Allow 2–3 hours. Easy independently. This is the simplest option for passengers who prefer to stay close to the ship. Start with the star-shaped Fuerte de San Diego, Acapulco's principal historic monument, then continue along the waterfront to the Zócalo and the Cathedral of Our Lady of Solitude.

The fort houses the Museo Histórico de Acapulco, although individual galleries can occasionally be temporarily unavailable. Check admission conditions at the entrance before planning a long museum visit.

La Quebrada Cliff Divers

Allow 2–3 hours. Independent by taxi with some planning. La Quebrada is Acapulco's signature attraction, where divers leap from cliffs approximately 35 m above the narrow Pacific inlet. The local tourism authority normally lists an early-afternoon performance around 13:00 as well as evening shows, but passengers should confirm the day's schedule before leaving the ship.

A taxi from the cruise port is the practical choice. There are steps and uneven sections around the viewing areas. Sinfonía del Mar, an open-air amphitheater overlooking the Pacific, is nearby and can easily be combined with the divers.

Caleta, Caletilla and Isla La Roqueta

Allow 3.5–5 hours. Independent with transport and careful timing. Take a taxi approximately 3.5 km (2.2 mi) from the cruise terminal to the traditional Caleta/Caletilla beach area. These protected beaches generally have calmer water than Acapulco's exposed Pacific beaches.

Boats leave from this area for Isla La Roqueta. The crossing takes only a few minutes, and some boats have glass-bottom viewing sections. On the island, passengers can swim, snorkel or walk through the vegetation. The longer island trail is about 3 km (1.9 mi) and requires suitable footwear.

Do not make the island trip late in the port call. Boat departures, sea conditions and the taxi ride back to the terminal all need to be included in the return margin.

Scenic Bay Drive and Capilla de la Paz

Allow 3–4 hours. Taxi/private driver or organized excursion recommended. A drive around Acapulco Bay provides a broader impression of the resort than the historic center alone. Capilla de la Paz sits approximately 6 km (3.7 mi) from the cruise port on the hillside above Las Brisas and has extensive views across the bay.

This is not a practical walking destination. Combining the chapel, panoramic viewpoints, the Costera and La Quebrada works particularly well with a private driver or organized city tour. Traffic on the main coastal roads can be slow, so avoid an itinerary that returns close to sailing time.

Self-Guided Walking Tours

Easy: Fort, Waterfront and Zócalo

Distance: approximately 1.5–2 km (0.9–1.2 mi) round trip. Pure walking time: about 25–35 minutes. Recommended total time: 1.5–2.5 hours. Difficulty: Easy, although heat and busy road crossings can make the walk more tiring.

  1. Cruise terminal exit – begin on the downtown waterfront.
  2. Fuerte de San Diego – visit the fort and its historical museum if open.
  3. Malecón – continue along the waterfront toward central Acapulco.
  4. Zócalo / Plaza Álvarez – the traditional main square.
  5. Acapulco Cathedral – immediately beside the Zócalo.
  6. Return along the waterfront to the cruise terminal.

The route is concentrated close to the ship and is the most practical independent option for a short call. Allow extra time for the fort rather than extending the walk unnecessarily into unfamiliar neighborhoods.

Moderate: Old Acapulco to La Quebrada

Distance: approximately 4–5 km (2.5–3.1 mi) if walked as a round trip from the terminal. Pure walking time: about 70–90 minutes. Recommended total time: 3–4 hours including the diving show. Difficulty: Moderate, with hills, steps, strong sun and limited shade.

  1. Cruise terminal
  2. Fuerte de San Diego
  3. Zócalo
  4. Acapulco Cathedral
  5. La Quebrada
  6. Sinfonía del Mar

This longer route is suitable only for confident daytime walkers who have checked current local and ship guidance. A more practical version is to walk through the historic center and then take a taxi to La Quebrada, returning to the terminal by taxi after the show.

Beaches and Nature

For a straightforward beach stop, Caleta and Caletilla are more practical for cruise passengers than the distant beaches of Acapulco's Diamond Zone. They are close enough for a taxi transfer and are also the departure point for boats to Isla La Roqueta.

Pie de la Cuesta and the Coyuca Lagoon area offer beaches, lagoon scenery and boat trips farther northwest of central Acapulco. Because these require longer road transfers and leave less margin for delays, they are better treated as half-day organized excursions rather than improvised independent trips.

Practical Tips

  • The historic center is hot and exposed; carry water, sun protection and comfortable footwear even for the short walking route.
  • Use taxis or arranged transport for La Quebrada, beaches and hillside viewpoints if you do not want to walk through the wider city.
  • For Isla La Roqueta, confirm the return-boat arrangements before departing Caleta and leave substantial time for the taxi ride back to the port.
  • For destinations outside the central tourist area, an organized ship excursion or reputable prearranged tour is the more conservative option.
  • Keep a substantial return margin, particularly when using boats or traveling around the bay, where traffic can lengthen transfer times.
  • Because security conditions in Guerrero can change, check current government travel advice and any information provided by the cruise line before going ashore.
